name: Patent Filings
blurb:
This section tracks cumulative AI-related patent counts for 108 companies, ranking them by total portfolio size and charting how the combined total moves over time. It answers who is building the largest patent positions in AI, not who is inventing the most cutting-edge techniques right now, since raw filing counts favor large, long-established portfolios over newer, more selective filers.

The total is checked daily but only changes in step jumps every five to seven days, so it is best read as a periodically refreshed patent-database snapshot rather than a live daily count of new filings. Filing databases also lag actual invention by months given publication delays, and patent volume says nothing about which filings cover techniques that matter commercially or turn out to be defensible.

As of September 5, 2026, the tracked total stands at 312,470 AI-related patents across the 108 companies, up from 310,516 three weeks earlier, a gain of about 1,954 patents, or roughly 650 per week. Samsung leads by a wide margin with 108,943 patents, more than the next three companies combined, IBM at 69,827, Apple at 31,794, and Huawei at 27,442. Microsoft follows at 24,682. Further down, chip and model companies file far less by volume. NVIDIA holds 3,489, Meta 2,684, and Palantir 1,668, reflecting narrower but more targeted AI patent strategies. The count also tracks granted patents rather than pending applications, so it understates real activity for companies whose recent filings are still in prosecution and have not yet issued.

reading.body:
Patent volume clusters heavily in legacy hardware and conglomerate firms rather than in the compute-native companies driving modern AI, with Samsung, IBM, and Apple holding 55% of the tracked total while NVIDIA, the dominant AI chip manufacturer, holds less than 1.2%.

The gap reflects fundamental differences in filing strategy. Samsung and IBM accumulated their portfolios over decades across consumer electronics, enterprise software, and telecommunications before AI became a distinct category. They file broadly to defend existing product lines and market position. NVIDIA, Meta, and Palantir file narrowly on techniques they believe defensible or commercially critical, a posture that produces smaller counts but often higher specificity. Patent volume does not measure invention velocity or quality, only portfolio size.

For AI infrastructure specifically, this pattern obscures the actual relationship between patent position and scaling capability. A chip designer filing 3,489 patents on GPU architecture and software stacks may exert more constraint on AI deployment than a conglomerate with 100,000 patents spread across legacy domains. The data captures granted patents only, so recent filers at companies scaling compute infrastructure now will appear artificially small until their applications issue, potentially years after filing.

The stock of 312,470 patents grows at roughly 650 per week. This rate reflects the maturation of AI as a patent category rather than breakthrough velocity. The data does not indicate which patents cover techniques required for scaling, which face invalidation or prior art challenges, or which companies are filing defensively versus offensively to clear paths for their own deployment.
